item.title: NVision Quantum Technologies Expands into Molecular Quantum Computing with Photonic Integrated Architecture
item.description:
Curator's Take: This article matters because NVision’s move from hyperpolarized MRI into a photonic‑integrated molecular qubit platform introduces a hybrid approach that could combine the long spin coherence of organic molecules with the scalability of silicon photonics—an avenue few companies have pursued at this stage. By leveraging optically addressable spins deposited directly on a chip, NVision aims to create photonically entangled gates that sidestep some of the cryogenic overhead of superconducting qubits while still targeting fault‑tolerant architectures, echoing recent interest in room‑temperature spin‑photon interfaces from groups at MIT and Oxford. If the integration challenges can be tamed, the technology could accelerate quantum simulation of chemistry and materials by offering a more manufacturable path to large‑scale qubit arrays, though readers should note that coherence times and error rates for molecular spins remain an open question.

NVision Quantum Technologies is expanding from its commercial hyperpolarized MRI platform into quantum computing hardware with its new PIQC (Photonic Integrated Quantum Chip) molecular architecture. This strategy utilizes synthetic organic molecules with optically addressable spin states deposited on silicon photonic chips, aiming for a scalable, photonically-entangled gate architecture for fault-tolerant quantum computing. This expansion builds on their commercial success with their Polaris MRI systems and recent significant financing and project involvement. If these results translate to hardware, they could accelerate the timeline for running meaningful algorithms on modestly sized quantum processors, though real‑world noise and connectivity constraints will still need experimental validation.

Researchers from Google Quantum AI, Google DeepMind, and MIT have developed a modular quantum error correction (QEC) architecture that significantly reduces the physical qubit overhead required for quantum computing. This new approach, detailed in a technical manuscript on arXiv, utilizes modular hyperbolic codes to achieve over 30x savings in qubit overhead compared to standard 2D surface codes. The architecture allows for high encoding rates without complex on-chip wiring, demonstrating high tolerance to noise in simulations. item.title: Discovering state-of-the-art quantum circuits with large language models
item.description:
Curator's Take: This article shows that large language models can act as creative partners in quantum circuit design, automatically generating reversible architectures that beat the best hand‑crafted solutions on most benchmark tasks. By coupling an LLM proposer with a rigorous evaluator, the authors demonstrate a scalable way to explore the vast space of Toffoli‑efficient circuits—a bottleneck that has limited practical algorithm deployment on near‑term hardware. The approach could accelerate the discovery of low‑overhead primitives for chemistry, optimization and number‑theoretic applications, though its success still depends on high‑quality evaluation metrics and may require further tuning to handle larger, more complex problems.

Significant efforts are currently being directed toward the implementation of large-scale quantum information processors, but realizing useful quantum advantage also requires the development of efficient quantum algorithms. While for many practical problems the dominant resource costs are associated with a small set of computational primitives, optimizing them in the quantum setting presents unique challenges, including a reversibility constraint absent from ordinary classical computation. Here we introduce an evolutionary framework in which large language models (LLMs) propose circuit designs and an independent evaluator verifies and scores them. We apply this framework to tasks spanning numerical computation, chemistry, optimization, quantum simulation, and number theory. In seven of the eight tasks, the discovered circuits significantly reduce both Toffoli and qubit counts relative to the state of the art. In the eighth, the search discovers a new reversible architecture for prime-field modular inversion. By handling reversibility differently, the architecture makes divsteps -- a classical algorithm previously impractical for reversible integer arithmetic -- viable and substantially improves the Toffoli-qubit trade-off for modular inversion. These results open the door for evaluator-guided LLM co-design of new algorithmic structures for quantum computation.

Read original at arXiv Quantum Physics
item.author: Mark Eatherly

item.title: SynDebug: A Framework to Debug Logic Bugs in Fault-Tolerant Quantum Computing Programs
item.description:
Curator's Take: This article marks the first demonstration of a systems‑level debugging framework that works inside encoded fault‑tolerant quantum programs, filling a glaring gap left by earlier tools that only inspected logical circuits. By embedding lightweight assertion primitives directly into surface‑code–style QEC layers with an average depth penalty of just 1.8 % and no detectable rise in logical error rates, SynDebug makes it feasible to catch logic bugs before they explode into costly runtime failures—a crucial step as experimental groups move from small prototypes toward scalable FTQC architectures. The work dovetails with recent advances in real‑time syndrome processing and could accelerate the development cycle for large‑scale algorithms such as Shor’s or quantum chemistry, though its current validation is largely simulation‑based and will need hardware trials to confirm performance under realistic noise.

Fault-tolerant quantum computing (FTQC) introduces substantial systems-level complexity through quantum error correction (QEC), making debugging FTQC programs challenging. Existing quantum debugging approaches primarily target logical-level circuits and do not naturally support debugging within realistic FTQC execution flows. We present SynDebug, the first systems-level debugging framework for FTQC programs. SynDebug introduces lightweight assertion-based debugging primitives that operate directly within encoded FTQC infrastructures while avoiding additional logical surface area and minimizing temporal overhead. We evaluate SynDebug across multiple QEC code families, code distances, and encoded workloads, including state preparation, entanglement validation, and Shor-style programs. Our results demonstrate that SynDebug enables practical FTQC debugging with an average 1.8% additional circuit depth overhead (0% in most cases) and no measurable increase in the logical error rate, showing that systems-level debugging for large-scale FTQC applications is both feasible and practical.

item.title: Programmable all-to-all entangling gates for cavity-coupled atoms
item.description:
Curator's Take: This article demonstrates a cavity‑mediated Mølmer‑Sørensen gate that gives neutral‑atom qubits genuine all‑to‑all connectivity without shuttling atoms with optical tweezers, a long‑standing bottleneck for scaling up atom arrays. By leveraging the shared photonic mode and local laser addressing, the authors achieve >99 % fidelity while suppressing motional errors, bringing neutral‑atom platforms closer to the error‑rates needed for fault‑tolerant codes such as the surface code. The approach also dovetails with recent advances in Rydberg‑mediated gates and cavity QED, suggesting a clear path toward modular, high‑connectivity quantum processors that can be programmed on demand.

Fault tolerant quantum computers greatly benefit from having both high fidelity entangling gates and a non-local qubit connectivity. However, most entangling gates for neutral atoms are local, requiring separated atoms to be moved using optical tweezers to yield entanglement between them. Here, we design a high fidelity Mølmer Sørensen-like entangling gate between neutral atoms coupled to a photonic cavity, enabling a programmable all-to-all connectivity through the shared cavity coupling. The gate is both robust to changes in cavity photon number, and enables selective entanglement between any subset of separated atoms through local laser addressing. This eliminates the need to physically move atoms to perform the gate, and therefore motional errors and erasure are suppressed. Using experimentally realistic parameters we demonstrate gate fidelities exceeding $F > 0.99$, with higher fidelities achievable through optimal control of the pump amplitudes.

item.title: Efficient quantum simulation of unitary gates based on atomic ensembles
item.description:
Curator's Take: This article shows that permutation‑symmetric atomic ensembles can be turned into an efficient “qudit” platform by using a Cartan‑decomposition of the spin Hamiltonian, yielding compact circuits built from collective spin operations. By demonstrating zero‑error evolution that stays independent of atom number—unlike Suzuki‑Trotter methods whose errors grow with system size—the work offers a scalable route to high‑fidelity quantum simulation on near‑term hardware. The result could dramatically reduce gate depth for many‑body simulations, making larger ensemble‑based processors experimentally viable.

We develop a technique to perform efficient unitary time evolution of a general spin Hamiltonian based on the system with identical qubits, as naturally realized by permutation symmetric atomic ensembles. We employ Cartan decomposition method to the associated Hamiltonian Lie algebra and construct the symmetry adapted generators to implement unitary operator of the ensemble Hamiltonian. This enables the compact circuit representations of the system dynamics in terms of experimentally accessible collective spin operations and exploits the Dicke basis structure of the ensembles as an effective qudit representation. We benchmark Cartan based evolution against both exact time evolution and the Suzuki Trotter product formula. Our results show that the Cartan protocol accurately reproduces the operator dynamics, spin expectation values, and fluctuation observables with zero error that are substantially smaller than those obtained through Trotterization while maintaining an optimized circuit structure. In addition, scaling analysis with the ensemble size demonstrates that the Cartan error remains independent of the atom number while the corresponding Trotter error increases with the system size, highlighting the improved efficiency of the Cartan approach for a larger system size.

Read original at arXiv Quantum Physics
item.author: Mark Eatherly

item.title: Classification of bipartite observables III: simplicity, mixtures and quantum error correction
item.description:
Curator's Take: This article shows that the infinite‑qubit Pauli group—central to stabilizer error correction—is mathematically the Fraïssé limit of finite alternating spaces, making it the exact analogue of the random graph in model theory. By interpreting simplicity theory as a language for quantum error correction, the authors reveal how Clifford circuits embody homogeneity, forking captures logical errors, and the Kim‑Pillay independence theorem mirrors syndrome gluing, offering a fresh logical toolkit for designing and analysing stabilizer codes. The work bridges abstract logic with practical QEC, suggesting new ways to reason about code structure and robustness while highlighting that once mixed preparations are allowed both frameworks acquire the tree property of the second kind, a subtle distinction that could inform future fault‑tolerant architectures.

The paradigm of a simple unstable theory in the sense of Shelah is the theory of the random graph, the Fraïssé limit of the finite graphs. Quantum error correction has a paradigm of its own, and we show that it is the counterpart of the random graph: the Pauli group on countably many qubits, taken modulo phases and with commutation as its relation, is the Fraïssé limit of the finite alternating spaces over the two-element field, and its form computes the syndromes of stabilizer codes. Seen through this correspondence, simplicity theory turns out to be a theory of error correction. Clifford encoding circuits implement the homogeneity of the Pauli group, forking recognizes the logical errors, and the independence theorem of Kim and Pillay is the gluing of syndromes. The two paradigms look alike as first-order structures, and they part company only when observables enter. Each defines a bipartite observable, and we prove that, once preparations are mixed, both acquire the tree property of the second kind in real-valued logic. They reach it by different roads, however, and we show that the probes decide which. The probes of the Pauli observable are the Pauli channels; for them the indicator of each syndrome sector is the difference of the responses of two uniform mixtures, and actual mixtures already witness the tree. The probes of the Rado observable see only marginals; conditions given by actual mixtures remain compatible on disjoint blocks, and the tree must be sought among idealized preparations.

Read original at arXiv Quantum Physics
item.author: Mark Eatherly

item.title: Energetics of Fault-Tolerant Spin-Qubit Quantum Computation
item.description:
Curator's Take: This article is the first systematic accounting of how much power a fault‑tolerant silicon spin‑qubit processor would actually consume, showing that cryogenic cooling dominates the baseline budget and that control‑signal multiplexing can cut total energy by two orders of magnitude. By comparing the quantum Fourier transform to its classical FFT counterpart, the authors demonstrate that a quantum device could become energetically competitive well before it overtakes classical hardware in runtime—a key insight for scaling strategies that have so far focused almost exclusively on speed. The work ties together recent advances in isotopically purified silicon qubits and surface‑code error correction, providing designers with concrete targets for control electronics and cooling infrastructure as the field moves toward million‑qubit systems.

Semiconductor spin qubits offer a promising route to compact and scalable quantum computers, combining long coherence times in isotopically purified silicon with compatibility with semiconductor manufacturing. Beyond computational speedup, their energy efficiency is an important consideration for future large-scale systems. We evaluate the power and energy requirements of a Loss-DiVincenzo spin-qubit quantum computer by analyzing the Quantum Fourier Transform (QFT) and benchmarking it against the classical Fast Fourier Transform (FFT). We develop a detailed energy budget, identifying cryogenic cooling as the dominant baseline contribution before quantum error correction (QEC). The comparison between the QFT and the classical FFT reveals that, for any quantum workload operating under a polynomially bounded sampling regime, the crossover in energy consumption occurs at smaller problem sizes than the crossover in execution time. Thus, quantum computing can become energetically competitive before achieving a speedup in execution time. We then incorporate surface-code QEC and analyze the energy costs of QEC cycles, gate synthesis, and decoding. At scale, instrumentation and decoding become dominant contributions, while cryogenic cooling imposes a constraint on scalability. We show that optimizing the control-signal demultiplexing ratio can reduce the overall energy cost by approximately two orders of magnitude. For a system with about one million physical qubits, we estimate a power consumption of approximately 100 kW, at least one order of magnitude below that of today's highest-performance classical computing systems.

Read original at arXiv Quantum Physics
item.author: Mark Eatherly

item.title: Connectivity Bounds for GHZ Graphs
item.description:
Curator's Take: This article settles a key open question about how the topology of photonic‑based GHZ experiments limits the dimensionality of multipartite entanglement, showing that vertex connectivity alone caps the achievable GHZ dimension by 2^{κ−1}+C(κ,2). By linking graph‑theoretic connectivity to concrete hardware constraints, the result narrows the search space for high‑dimensional GHZ sources and explains why many recent attempts have stalled at low dimensions. The bounds also give experimental designers a practical metric—improving network robustness directly translates into higher‑dimensional entanglement potential, though the limits still leave room for clever graph constructions to push beyond current records.

Greenberger-Horne-Zeilinger (GHZ) states are multipartite entangled quantum states that play a central role in quantum information theory, with applications in quantum communication, cryptography, and distributed quantum computing. A major experimental goal is to create high-dimensional GHZ states using multiple entangled parties. Krenn, Gu and Zeilinger discovered a surprising bridge between these quantum-optical experiments and graph theory: certain photonic experiments can be represented by edge-coloured, edge-weighted graphs, and the dimension of the produced GHZ state equals the number of feasible monochromatic inherited vertex colourings. This led Krenn and Gu to conjecture that every GHZ graph with more than four vertices has dimension at most $2$. A counterexample would give a new high-dimensional multipartite GHZ construction, while a proof would clarify fundamental resource limitations in quantum optics. It is known that the conjecture holds for graphs of vertex connectivity at most $2$ [MFCS 2024], and that simple GHZ graphs with $n>4$ vertices have dimension less than $n/\sqrt{2}$ [Quantum 2024]. However, no general upper bound depending only on vertex connectivity was known. We prove that every simple connected GHZ graph $G$ with at least four vertices has dimension at most $2^{κ(G)-1}+\binom{κ(G)}{2}$, where $κ(G)$ is the vertex connectivity of $G$. We also prove new bounds in terms of edge connectivity and maximum degree.

item.description:

By spotlighting Falcon‑512 as a compact, high‑throughput signature scheme, Terra Quantum bridges recent PQC standardization efforts with the practical constraints of ledger scalability—a gap that has been largely unaddressed in prior cryptography research. The analysis also contextualizes emerging proposals such as Ethereum’s EIP‑8052 and Solana’s WOTS vaults, giving developers a realistic timeline for upgrading security before large‑scale quantum computers become viable.

A white paper by Terra Quantum AG analyzes the vulnerability of major blockchain platforms like Bitcoin, Ethereum, and Solana to post-quantum cryptography (PQC) threats, highlighting the risks posed by Shor's algorithm to digital signature algorithms. The study evaluates PQC migration strategies, emphasizing signature payload size as a critical factor for high-throughput ledgers, and suggests FN-DSA (Falcon-512) as a viable solution due to its compact signature footprint. The paper also reviews mitigation frameworks, including Solana's WOTS vaults, Algorand's Falcon account roadmaps, and Ethereum's EIP-8052 proposal. item.title: Patchwork: automated lattice surgery and space-time partitioning for real-time decoding
item.description:
Curator's Take: This article matters because it delivers the first fully automated compiler—Patchwork—that can translate arbitrary multi‑qubit Pauli measurements into concrete lattice‑surgery operations on a realistic narrow‑corridor surface‑code layout, while preserving the full code distance even for logical Y measurements using twist defects. By introducing a wavefront partitioning scheme that separates commit, buffer and cleanup regions, the authors enable parallel, real‑time decoding whose failure rates closely match those of traditional monolithic decoders, addressing a major bottleneck in scaling fault‑tolerant processors. Together these tools bring practical, low‑latency error correction one step closer to large‑scale quantum computers that can run complex algorithms without prohibitive overhead.

We introduce patchwork, a lattice-surgery compiler for arbitrary multi-qubit Pauli measurements on a prescribed narrow-corridor two-dimensional surface-code layout. Systematic geometric rules simplify stabilizer placement and gate scheduling, including for logical $Y$ measurements implemented using twist defects. We introduce measurement circuits and schedules that, together with protruding lobes of $Y$-extension patches, preserve the full effective code distance for all numerically tested code distances. To support parallel decoding, we develop a wavefront algorithm that partitions merged lattice-surgery patches into space-time commit, buffer, and cleanup regions. Simulations of three sequential multi-qubit Pauli measurements acting on ten logical qubits show that staged decoding achieves total failure probabilities close to those of monolithic decoding over the parameters tested. These methods provide an automated framework for fault-tolerant lattice surgery and a route toward scalable, real-time decoding.

item.title: Operational Limits of Gravity-Mediated Entanglement
item.description:
Curator's Take: This article pinpoints the practical limits that finite‑size wave packets and stray forces impose on proposed gravity‑mediated entanglement experiments, moving the discussion from idealized point‑mass models toward realistic laboratory conditions. By quantifying when the generated state remains Bell‑nonlocal or useful for teleportation, it provides concrete design tolerances that complement recent tabletop proposals such as the Bose–Marletto–Vedral scheme and upcoming optomechanical tests. The finding that even a modest electrostatic coupling can cancel the gravitational phase underscores why meticulous shielding will be essential before any claim of witnessing quantum gravity can be made.

Tests of gravity-mediated entanglement aim to determine whether two massive objects in spatial superposition can become entangled through their mutual gravitational interaction. In an ideal model, the two objects are often treated as pointlike branches, but real wave packets have a finite width and are also exposed to dephasing and residual non-gravitational forces. We study these effects in a two-branch gravitational cat-state model with Gaussian wave packets. The Newtonian interaction is averaged over the finite wave-packet width, and spatially correlated dephasing is included phenomenologically. We then ask a practical question: when does the generated state remain useful rather than merely entangled? To answer this, we examine Bell violation, teleportation fidelity, coherent information, Fisher information, and state distinguishability. We find finite parameter windows where the same state is Bell-nonlocal and teleportation-useful, but these windows shrink as the wave packets become broader or the dephasing becomes stronger. We also show that a residual electrostatic branch interaction can coherently cancel the gravitational nonlocal phase and strongly suppress the operational signal. The results identify finite-width and electrostatic tolerance boundaries that should be considered in future tests of gravity-mediated entanglement.

item.title: Quantum control of solid state qubits via Reinforcement Learning
item.description:
Curator's Take: This article demonstrates that model‑free reinforcement learning can reliably discover high‑fidelity pulse sequences for indirect control of NV nuclear spins even when the surrounding spin bath is modeled with realistic many‑body noise, a regime where traditional analytic or gradient‑based methods struggle. By benchmarking RL against other black‑box optimizers on sparse, noisy reward signals, the authors show that AI‑driven control can match or exceed state‑of‑the‑art performance without any prior knowledge of the device Hamiltonian—a crucial step toward autonomous calibration of NISQ hardware. The work broadens the recent wave of RL applications from superconducting circuits to solid‑state spin platforms, suggesting a path toward scalable, noise‑robust quantum gate synthesis for emerging quantum sensors and processors.

The use of reinforcement learning (RL) in the design of quantum control strategies for pulse level control of NISQ era quantum devices is attracting growing interest. Model-free RL, not requiring preexisting knowledge of the physical system, acts as a black-box optimization tool well suited for noisy devices. In this work, we provide a simulation-based analysis of the performance of model-free RL for state preparation and qubit gate design in a challenging setup: indirect control of NV nuclear spins in a spin-bath. In particular, the spin-bath is modeled via the generalized cluster correlation expansion accounting for magnetic impurities and intra-bath interactions. We analyze the performance of the RL agents by performing simulations with minimally observable environments and noisy, sparse rewards as introduced in (Phys. Rev. X 12, 011059), and compare them to other state-of-the-art black-box optimization tools.

item.title: Jianmu-Q: Bridging Quantum Field Theory and Quantum Hardware with AI Agents
item.description:
Curator's Take: This article showcases Jianmu‑Q, the first multi‑agent AI framework that converts a natural‑language description of a quantum field theory into a full quantum‑simulation workflow—including lattice discretization, qubit mapping and circuit synthesis—while continuously cross‑checking against classical exact‑diagonalisation and tensor‑network results. By demonstrating end‑to‑end validation on benchmark models up to (2+1)‑dimensional gauge theories and even running selected circuits on IBM hardware, the work bridges a long‑standing gap between high‑energy theory and near‑term quantum processors. The approach could dramatically lower the expertise barrier for researchers wanting to explore non‑perturbative QFT dynamics on quantum devices, though its current reliance on noiseless simulations means further hardware error mitigation will be needed before large‑scale studies become routine.

Quantum computing offers a promising approach to non-perturbative simulations of quantum field theories, particularly for real-time dynamics and systems affected by the sign problem. Yet translating continuum field theories into quantum computations remains a challenging interdisciplinary task. Here we introduce \texttt{Jianmu-Q}, a multi-agent framework that transforms natural-language descriptions of quantum field theories into quantum simulation workflows. Specialized agents handle theoretical formulation, lattice discretization, qubit mapping, and circuit design, while physical consistency checks and independent numerical calculations provide validation throughout the workflow. We benchmark the framework on three field theories of increasing complexity: the $(1+1)$-dimensional Nambu--Jona-Lasinio and Schwinger models, and a $(2+1)$-dimensional $\mathbb{Z}_2$ gauge theory. Across these systems, noiseless quantum-circuit simulations converge toward independent exact-diagonalization and tensor-network results, while selected circuits are executed on IBM quantum hardware, demonstrating an end-to-end, validation-guided approach to quantum simulation of field theories.

item.title: ZZ-Free bSWAP Gates under Strong Driving in Far-Detuned Fixed-Frequency Transmons
item.description:
Curator's Take: This article shows that a strong single‑tone drive can generate a clean XX–YY interaction in far‑detuned fixed‑frequency transmons, enabling a 150 ns √bSWAP gate that creates maximally entangled states without the unwanted ZZ phase. By pairing the strong drive with a weak second tone to cancel the residual ZZ, the authors achieve a SWAP operation 33 % faster than conventional cross‑resonance CNOTs while maintaining higher interleaved randomized benchmarking fidelity, highlighting a practical path to speed up two‑qubit gates on spectrally crowded processors. The work also demonstrates two‑axis counter‑twisting squeezing, suggesting that the newly accessible interaction can be leveraged for both more efficient gate synthesis and analog quantum simulation of spin models—though its advantage hinges on careful calibration of drive amplitudes and may require hardware with sufficient anharmonicity to avoid leakage.

Far-detuned frequency allocations in fixed-frequency superconducting processors mitigate spectral crowding but constrain cross-resonance interactions at practical drive amplitudes. Here, we demonstrate that a single strong drive induces a large $XX-YY$ interaction in the far-detuned regime, while a weak second tone tunes the accompanying $ZZ$ phase. The interaction realizes a 150-ns $\sqrt{\mathrm{bSWAP}}$ gate, which can directly prepare a maximally entangled state from the ground state. For the implementations on the same qubit pair at matched drive strengths, cross resonance gives a shorter CNOT operation, while $\sqrt{\mathrm{bSWAP}}$ gives a 33% shorter SWAP operation with a higher IRB fidelity. The multilevel theory further predicts a regime where stronger driving can yield a speed advantage for CNOT as well, a possibility absent in the two-level model. As an application of the $XX-YY$ interaction, we also demonstrate two-spin squeezing beyond the standard quantum limit through two-axis countertwisting. The interaction realized here complements cross resonance and offers a route to efficient gate synthesis and quantum simulation of interacting spin systems.

item.title: Looking Beyond Visibility: Resolving the Temporal Structure of Continuous-Wave Four-Photon Hong-Ou-Mandel Interference
item.description:
Curator's Take: This article demonstrates a new way to capture the full temporal dynamics of continuous‑wave four‑photon Hong‑Ou‑Mandel interference, moving beyond the traditional single‑visibility metric by recording every photon’s arrival time and visualising it in a three‑dimensional coincidence histogram. By leveraging long‑coherence microring resonators and ultrafast detectors, the authors provide a practical benchmark that lets experimenters optimise the trade‑off between visibility and count rate after data collection—a capability increasingly valuable as integrated photonic platforms scale toward quantum networking and repeater applications. The approach highlights both the promise of richer time‑resolved diagnostics for CW sources and the current need for high‑performance timing hardware to fully exploit it.

Hong-Ou-Mandel interference underpins many photonic quantum information protocols and is commonly characterized by a single visibility parameter. This quantity is typically obtained by averaging over a fixed coincidence window, thereby discarding details of the underlying temporal structure that are critical in continuous-wave processes. Four-photon interference with continuous-wave sources furthermore requires photon pairs with long coherence times, which we generate in microring resonators and measure with ultrafast time-resolved detection. Here, we model and resolve their interference and temporal structure by recording all four photon arrival times and mapping their relative delays onto a three-dimensional coincidence histogram relative to a trigger detection. The resulting structure preserves relative arrival-time correlations that are usually discarded and enables post-processed optimization of coincidence windows to trade off visibility against count rate. This method provides a general benchmark for continuous-wave sources in interference-based quantum network protocols.

item.title: Superconducting circuits host two-level systems with lifetimes exceeding one second
item.description:
Curator's Take: This article shows that parasitic two‑level systems in superconducting circuits can live for more than a second—orders of magnitude longer than even the best transmon qubits—by using wide‑band quantum‑jump spectroscopy to isolate their intrinsic decay. By revealing such ultra‑stable microscopic defects, the work turns a traditional source of decoherence into a potential resource for error‑correction monitoring and high‑resolution sensing, echoing recent efforts to harness “quiet” ancillae for fault‑tolerant architectures. The findings also demonstrate that superconducting qubits can serve as exquisitely sensitive probes of hidden material dynamics, although the exact nature of these long‑lived TLSs (whether tunneling defects, spins or quasiparticles) remains an open question.

Understanding the microscopic environment of superconducting qubits is a central challenge for quantum technologies. Parasitic two-level systems (TLSs) of various microscopic origins are ubiquitous and limit qubit performance through decoherence, frequency drifts, and leakage. Recently, long-lived TLSs with lifetimes exceeding those of state-of-the-art qubits have been shown to induce correlated qubit dynamics, with direct implications for quantum error correction. Here, we perform wide-band quantum-jump correlation spectroscopy on flux-tunable transmon qubits and identify microscopic degrees of freedom that outlive the qubit by orders of magnitude. Pump-probe measurements at varying detunings from these objects reveal intrinsic lifetimes exceeding one second. Their weak coupling to the qubit, in the kilohertz range, is consistent with positional defects described by the standard tunneling model, without excluding other microscopic origins such as magnetic spin impurities or trapped quasiparticles. More broadly, these results establish superconducting qubits as a sensitive probe of exceptionally long-lived microscopic degrees of freedom and open a route toward their controlled access and functionalization.

item.title: Same Spectrum, Harder First-Order Training: Phase-Locking in Single- versus Multi-Qubit Re-Uploading Circuits
item.description:
Curator's Take: This article shows that although a single‑qubit re‑uploading circuit can mathematically reproduce any function a multi‑qubit encoder of the same budget can, its gradient landscape is severely constrained by “phase‑locking,” giving it far fewer independent tangent directions for first‑order optimization. The result explains why many near‑term quantum‑machine‑learning proposals that favor ultra‑narrow, deep circuits may suffer dramatically slower convergence compared with modestly wider multi‑qubit designs—a trade‑off echoed in recent studies of expressivity versus trainability and barren‑plateau phenomena. Practically, the work suggests developers should be cautious about swapping width for depth alone and consider hybrid architectures or richer encodings to ensure reliable training on real hardware.

Angle-encoded variational quantum circuits implement truncated Fourier series. For one-dimensional inputs, a single-qubit re-uploading (serial) circuit represents every function that a multi-qubit circuit with the same encoding budget $E$ can; we find that this exchange of width for depth is not free in first-order training. Because its state lives on the Bloch sphere, all parameters of the serial circuit move the state, at each input, along one complex direction, which we call \emph{phase-locking}. We prove that this costs no Fourier direction but leaves no direction to spare: however many parameters it has, the serial circuit has at most $2E+2$ tangent directions, one more than its $2E+1$ Fourier coefficients need, while a two-qubit control with the same encoding budget and model class generically has at least $6E+6$. The cost in training is measured against this control, as the number of runs out of 100 that reach the optimum within a fixed step budget. On an exact loss with flat-spectrum targets the gap grows with $E$; at $E=32$ the serial circuit converges in 3, 53 and 83 runs under gradient descent, Adam and Levenberg--Marquardt, the control in 99, 100 and 100. On three real-world series, at matched parameter counts, the serial circuit reaches the least-squares optimum in at most 9 runs under Adam and in 32 to 93 under Levenberg--Marquardt, the control in at least 98 and in all 100; its held-out error is up to about $1.5$ times that of the control under Adam, but no larger in the typical run under Levenberg--Marquardt.

item.title: Probing Deconfined Quantum Criticality Point on a Digital Quantum Computer
item.description:
Curator's Take: This article shows that a noisy superconducting quantum processor can faithfully capture the subtle signatures of a deconfined quantum critical point—a Landau‑forbidden phase transition that has long been a benchmark for many‑body theory. By combining ancilla‑projected quantum imaginary‑time evolution with tensor‑network compression, the authors achieve shallow circuits whose hardware measurements reproduce order‑parameter crossings and correlation ratios in line with state‑of‑the‑art classical simulations. The work demonstrates that near‑term devices are already capable of probing exotic critical phenomena, opening a practical pathway for quantum simulators to explore physics beyond conventional symmetry‑breaking paradigms while still contending with finite‑size and noise limitations.

A deconfined quantum critical point (DQCP) is a continuous transition between ordered phases with unrelated broken symmetries, beyond the Landau-Ginzburg-Wilson paradigm. In one dimension, such a transition between a $z$-polarized ferromagnet (zFM) and a valence-bond solid (VBS) is well established numerically in a frustrated spin-$1/2$ chain. Here we ask whether a superconducting quantum processor can resolve this transition and its signatures despite finite-size effects and device noise. The ground states are prepared by ancilla-projected quantum imaginary-time evolution (QITE), whose exact target states are compressed by tensor-network optimization into shallow depth quantum circuits. The hardware data distinguish the phases through their order parameters, spin and dimer correlations, structure factors, correlation ratios, and snapshot distributions. The crossing of the order parameters locates the transition, and its finite-size extrapolation lies close to the thermodynamic-limit value obtained from large-scale numerics. A noise model based on the device calibration accounts quantitatively for the reduced amplitudes measured on hardware. Our findings demonstrate that a Landau-forbidden transition between competing orders can be resolved on current quantum processors.

item.title: Remote Gottesman-Kitaev-Preskill Entanglement Generation between Trapped Ions
item.description:
Curator's Take: This article demonstrates a practical route to entangle error‑corrected GKP logical qubits across separate trapped‑ion modules using heralded photon links, moving the field beyond proof‑of‑concept demonstrations of raw physical‑qubit networking. By leveraging already‑tested motional‑control and photonic interfacing techniques, the authors show that realistic imperfections still permit logical Bell‑pair fidelities above 95 %, a threshold that could enable fault‑tolerant distributed quantum computing. The work ties together recent progress in modular ion traps and bosonic error correction, suggesting that scalable quantum networks may soon be built from hardware that already exists in many labs.

Distributing entanglement directly between error-corrected logical qubits is an important capability for scalable quantum networks. We propose a heralded protocol for generating remote entanglement between Gottesman--Kitaev--Preskill qubits encoded in the motional modes of spatially separated trapped ions, using the internal electronic states to interface the motional qubits with emitted photons. We derive the protocol for single-rail and polarization photonic encodings and evaluate the effects of finite GKP squeezing, photon loss, photon recoil, motional heating, and motional dephasing on the decoded logical state. Moreover, we numerically analysed the fidelity of distributed logical Bell-pair fidelity. We find that one can achieve more than 95% of fidelity in the realistic situation. The protocol combines motional-control and photonic-networking operations that have already been demonstrated in trapped-ion experiments.

item.title: Realization Divergence in Multi-Provider Quantum Computing: A Pre-Registered Study of What Survives Measurement
item.description:
Curator's Take: This article shines a light on “realization divergence,” the often‑overlooked gap between a quantum program’s source code and what actually runs on different hardware stacks—a factor that can dominate error budgets even before physical noise is considered. By pre‑registering predictions across three vendors and showing how placement policies, embedding radius and circuit topology systematically reshape outcomes, the study provides concrete evidence that software‑level choices are as critical as qubit fidelity for reproducible performance. The findings reinforce recent calls for standardized compilation benchmarks and transparent stack reporting, reminding developers and policymakers that cross‑provider comparability hinges on both hardware advances and disciplined software engineering.

Quantum programs pass through compilers, transpilers and vendor services before execution. However, the distance between what was written and what runs is rarely measured. We call this distance realization divergence: the observable difference in how an identical source circuit is realized and behaves across quantum software stacks. We report a hardware study across three vendors and four devices, combining pre-registered predictions with explicitly identified exploratory analyses and amendments. In a compilation experiment with assigned placement policies, embedding radius correlates with two-qubit overhead at Spearman 0.805, against 0.492 for circuit size. Under a fixed lowest-index policy, an eight-qubit Bernstein-Vazirani circuit exhibits greater execution divergence than a twelve-qubit circuit on IQM Emerald. The opposite ordering occurs on IQM Garnet. Both comparisons replicate across two repetitions with disjoint confidence intervals. These results support a placement-dependent explanation, without isolating individual hardware noise mechanisms. The same ordering inversion is absent on the all-to-all IonQ control. On Rigetti Cepheus, a follow-up using topology-aware native placement found no consistent advantage in correct-answer probability for either submission track, but did not establish equivalence between the tracks. Structural comparisons depend on metric weighting, placement and device generation. Provider interfaces also limit observability: Rigetti's supported-operation list remained unchanged across a device generation that replaced the native entangler. We classify silent interface failures in composed toolchains and identify checks at toolchain boundaries, connecting valid cross-provider comparisons with concrete software-quality practices.

item.title: Simultaneous high-fidelity single-qubit gates in a spin qubit array
item.description:
Curator's Take: This article marks the first demonstration of simultaneous, high‑fidelity single‑qubit rotations across a five‑qubit silicon spin array, pushing gate fidelities into the error‑correction regime while operating all qubits in parallel. By showing that cross‑talk can be suppressed enough to maintain >99.9 % fidelity on each site, the work bridges the gap between isolated laboratory devices and scalable CMOS‑compatible processors that will need dozens or hundreds of concurrently driven spins. The result validates a key hardware requirement for fault‑tolerant architectures, though extending the technique to larger arrays and integrating fast two‑qubit gates remains an open challenge.

item.title: monoprop: Scaling Pauli and Majorana propagation via Anticommutation Indices
item.description:
Curator's Take: This article introduces a fundamentally faster way to propagate Pauli strings and Majorana operators by using an anticommutation index that reduces the per‑gate cost from O(KN) to O(K/N), meaning larger lattices can actually be simulated more quickly for a fixed operator budget. By demonstrating near‑ideal scaling on thousands of cores and providing memory‑efficient surrogate graphs for rapid energy re‑evaluation, monoprop opens the door to high‑fidelity, adaptive quantum‑chemistry simulations that were previously limited by classical overhead. As an open‑source, massively parallel framework it complements existing toolkits such as Qiskit and OpenFermion, giving researchers a practical route to explore far larger fermionic systems and gradient‑based circuit optimizations on today’s HPC resources.

We introduce monoprop, an open-source, massively parallel operator-propagation framework for fermion and qubit bases. For $N$ qubits or modes, existing codes represent each of the $K$ tracked operator terms (Pauli strings or products of Majorana operators) as a $2N$-bit string, testing each for anticommutation with the gate at $O(KN)$ cost per gate. Here, we introduce the anticommutation index which rapidly looks up the terms anticommuting with a gate. A local gate changes only the terms that touch its sites, and when terms are truncated to act on few sites, only a fraction $\sim1/N$ touch any given qubit or mode, and we use this to prove the time per gate scales as $O(K/N)$. This counterintuitive result tells us that for a fixed number of terms, increasing the number of sites can make things faster. We demonstrate this numerically, and show monoprop scales almost ideally to 8192 cores, tracking $9.5\times10^{10}$ terms. Beyond propagation, we present memory-efficient surrogate graphs, which record one propagation and replay it at new angles, for fast energy re-estimation and parameter gradients, and an efficient method for finding energy-minimising gates and optimal angles for simulating adaptive quantum-chemistry circuits.

item.title: Quantum-Aware Key Rank for Side-Channel Attacks evaluation
item.description:
Curator's Take: This article fills a crucial gap by giving side‑channel analysts a concrete framework for estimating how much advantage a quantum adversary would gain when finishing a key‑rank search on a quantum computer, something that has been missing from current evaluation pipelines. By showing that the quadratic Grover speedup only holds up to a depth‑limited rank threshold (around 2^58.6 for AES‑128 under today’s NIST MAXDEPTH budget) and then collapses to a modest constant factor, it provides realistic security margins for hardware designers who must now consider quantum‑aware key ranks alongside classical ones. The work also offers a practical metric that can be derived from existing post‑processing tools, enabling labs to quickly assess whether their devices remain safe against near‑term quantum‑enhanced side‑channel attacks.

Side-channel attacks on block ciphers rarely recover the key outright: they leave a residual key space ordered by subkey posteriors, and evaluation laboratories report the key rank of the true key against thresholds near 2^48 and 2^60. No evaluation framework models an adversary who collects traces classically and finishes the search on a quantum computer, although quantum search with advice provides exactly that. We give such an adversary a cost model and a metric. For a device whose key has rank r, any quantum algorithm with classical access to the posteriors needs Omega(sqrt(r)) cipher evaluations, and block search achieves O(sqrt(r)); the per-instance advantage is exactly quadratic, and the super-quadratic exponents reported for search with advice are averages over the prior that apply to no single device. Under the NIST MAXDEPTH budget D and a Grover iteration of g gates and depth d, the quadratic advantage holds only for ranks up to (4D/(pi d))^2 and collapses to a constant factor beyond; with the best published AES-128 oracle and D = 2^40 the window closes near rank 2^58.6. We define the quantum-aware key rank, the classical rank of equal cost, computable from the rank estimators laboratories already run, and derive the classical rank a device must retain to keep a given threshold against each depth budget. Block search and amplitude amplification from the product-form posterior state are within a factor of two to four of each other on Hamming-weight posteriors, so the cost of coherent indexing decides between them. Experiments on simulated leakage and a toy cipher confirm the predicted window: at SNR 0.125 a depth-limited quantum adversary is worth about 22 traces to a classical one, however large its gate budget.
